outputs.L3:
A lift device includes a chassis having a rear leveling assembly and a front leveling assembly coupled to opposite ends of the chassis. The rear leveling assembly is positioned at or near a rear end of the chassis, while the front leveling assembly is positioned at or near a front end of the chassis. Together, the leveling assemblies are configured to adjust the orientation of the chassis relative to a support surface, such as the ground, to improve stability and maintain a desired level condition during operation of the lift device.

The rear leveling assembly includes a first rear actuator and a second rear actuator. The first and second rear actuators are selectively engageable to provide active control of rear pitch and roll adjustments of the chassis. By independently controlling the rear actuators, the rear portion of the chassis can be raised, lowered, or tilted as needed to compensate for uneven terrain or changing load conditions. This active control allows the rear leveling assembly to precisely adjust the position and angular orientation of the chassis.

The front leveling assembly includes a first front actuator and a second front actuator. The first and second front actuators are configured to provide front pitch and roll adjustment of the chassis. In some operating modes, the front actuators can be selectively fluidly coupled to one another to provide passive front pitch and roll control. When fluidly coupled, movement of one front actuator may be hydraulically communicated to the other front actuator, allowing the front leveling assembly to respond passively to changes in terrain or chassis orientation.

In other operating modes, the first and second front actuators can be fluidly decoupled from one another to provide active front pitch and roll control. When decoupled, the front actuators may be independently controlled to actively raise, lower, or tilt the front portion of the chassis. This enables more precise adjustment of the chassis orientation when active leveling is desired.

Accordingly, the lift device provides a leveling system in which the rear leveling assembly is configured for active rear pitch and roll control, while the front leveling assembly is selectively configurable between a passive control mode and an active control mode. This arrangement allows the lift device to adapt to different operating conditions by providing passive compliance when appropriate and active leveling control when increased precision or stability is required.
outputs.L4:
A lift device is configured to improve chassis leveling by using coordinated front and rear leveling assemblies. The lift device includes a chassis supported by a plurality of ground-engaging members, such as wheels or tracks, and a lift structure mounted to the chassis. Because the stability and operation of the lift structure can be affected by uneven terrain, the lift device is provided with leveling systems that adjust the position of the chassis relative to the ground. These leveling systems allow the chassis to be adjusted in both pitch and roll directions so that the lift structure can be operated from a more stable and level platform.

The rear leveling assembly includes a pair of rear actuators positioned on opposite sides of the chassis. Each rear actuator is operable to raise or lower a corresponding rear portion of the chassis. By controlling the rear actuators together or independently, the system can adjust the pitch of the chassis, the roll of the chassis, or a combination of both. The rear actuators are configured for selective active control, meaning that each actuator may be deliberately driven to a desired position or force condition based on operator input, sensor feedback, or an automatic leveling command. This active control allows the rear of the chassis to be precisely positioned to compensate for uneven ground conditions.

The front leveling assembly includes a pair of front actuators positioned on opposite sides of the chassis. These front actuators are arranged to provide two different operating modes. In a passive mode, the front actuators are fluidly coupled to one another so that movement of one front actuator can cause corresponding movement of the other front actuator. This allows the front portion of the chassis to articulate or equalize in response to terrain variations, helping maintain contact with the ground and reducing undesirable stress on the chassis. The passive fluid-coupled mode can be useful when the lift device is traveling or when automatic compliance with the terrain is desired.

The front actuators can also be switched to an active mode in which they are decoupled from one another and controlled independently. In this mode, each front actuator may be actively extended or retracted to achieve a desired chassis orientation. Independent active control of the front actuators provides additional authority over chassis roll and pitch and allows the leveling system to make more precise adjustments when the lift device is positioned for lifting operations. The ability to selectively transition between passive coupled control and active decoupled control gives the lift device increased flexibility across different operating conditions.

By combining selectively active rear actuators with front actuators that can alternate between passive fluid-coupled operation and active independent operation, the lift device provides enhanced leveling performance. The system can allow compliant movement when needed, provide precise leveling when required, and improve overall stability during operation of the lift structure. This arrangement supports safer and more reliable use of the lift device on sloped, irregular, or otherwise uneven surfaces.

**The Power of “The”**

“The” is one of the smallest words in the English language, yet it plays an important role in communication. As a definite article, “the” helps us refer to something specific or already known. For example, when we say “the book,” we mean a particular book, not just any book.

This simple word gives clarity and direction to a sentence. It helps readers and listeners understand exactly what is being discussed. Without “the,” many sentences would feel incomplete or unclear. Whether used in everyday speech, writing, titles, or descriptions, “the” is essential for making language precise and meaningful.

Although it may seem ordinary, “the” is one of the most frequently used words in English. Its importance reminds us that even the smallest words can have a big impact.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a technical patent disclosure excerpt for a mobile lift device that uses two rear actuators for active rear leveling and two front actuators that can be fluidly coupled for passive leveling or decoupled for active leveling.
counterfactuals.output:
## Technical Disclosure Excerpt

A mobile lift device is disclosed having a chassis, a lift assembly supported by the chassis, a plurality of ground-engaging members, and a leveling system configured to maintain a platform or frame portion of the lift device within a selected angular range relative to gravity or relative to a reference plane. The lift device may be, for example, a mobile elevating work platform, boom lift, scissor lift, material lift, or other self-propelled or towable lifting apparatus.

In one embodiment, the mobile lift device includes a rear axle region having a left rear actuator and a right rear actuator. Each rear actuator is operatively connected between the chassis and a corresponding rear wheel support, suspension member, axle member, or outrigger-like support element. The left rear actuator and the right rear actuator are independently controllable to provide active rear leveling of the chassis. A controller receives inclination information from one or more sensors, such as an inertial measurement unit, accelerometer, tilt sensor, position sensor, pressure sensor, or actuator stroke sensor, and commands the rear actuators to extend or retract independently to reduce chassis roll, pitch, or a combined tilt condition.

The mobile lift device further includes a front axle region having a left front actuator and a right front actuator. The front actuators are operatively connected between the chassis and corresponding front wheel supports, suspension members, axle members, or ground-contacting support structures. The left front actuator and the right front actuator are selectively configurable between a fluidly coupled mode and a fluidly decoupled mode. In the fluidly coupled mode, working chambers of the left and right front actuators are connected by one or more fluid passages so that fluid may transfer between the front actuators in response to terrain variation. In this mode, the front actuators provide passive front leveling or passive axle articulation, allowing the front portion of the chassis to accommodate uneven ground while reducing the need for active control input. The fluid coupling may permit one front actuator to retract while the other front actuator extends, thereby maintaining wheel contact and distributing load across the front ground-engaging members.

In the fluidly decoupled mode, the fluid communication between the left front actuator and the right front actuator is restricted, blocked, or otherwise controlled such that each front actuator can be driven independently. In this mode, the controller may actively command the front actuators to extend or retract to provide active front leveling. The front actuators may be decoupled by one or more valves, including solenoid valves, proportional valves, check valves, pilot-operated valves, or a valve manifold configured to isolate corresponding actuator chambers. When decoupled, the controller may use the front actuators together with the rear actuators to control chassis attitude, increase stability, compensate for slope, prepare the lift assembly for elevation, or maintain a desired platform orientation during travel or lifting operations.

The leveling system may include a hydraulic circuit having a pump, reservoir, accumulator, valve manifold, and conduits coupled to the four actuators. The two rear actuators may be connected to individually controlled valve sections to enable independent active control. The two front actuators may be connected through a selectable cross-coupling circuit. The selectable cross-coupling circuit may include a coupling valve movable between an open state, in which corresponding chambers of the front actuators are fluidly connected, and a closed state, in which the corresponding chambers are isolated. In certain embodiments, the front actuators are double-acting cylinders, and both cap-end chambers and rod-end chambers may be selectively coupled or isolated. In other embodiments, only one set of chambers is selectively coupled while the opposite chambers are connected to a controlled supply, return, accumulator, or load-holding arrangement.

The controller may select the coupled or decoupled state of the front actuators based on operating mode, vehicle speed, lift height, chassis tilt, sensed load, ground slope, outrigger deployment state, steering angle, or operator command. For example, during travel over uneven terrain with the lift assembly stowed, the controller may place the front actuators in the fluidly coupled mode to allow passive articulation and improved ground contact. When the lift assembly is raised above a threshold height, when the chassis is stationary, or when a leveling command is received, the controller may place the front actuators in the decoupled mode and actively control one or more of the front actuators in coordination with the rear actuators. In some embodiments, the rear actuators remain actively controlled while the front actuators are in the coupled mode, such that active rear leveling is combined with passive front leveling.

A method of leveling the mobile lift device may include sensing an inclination of the chassis, independently actuating the left rear actuator and the right rear actuator to reduce the sensed inclination, and selecting a front actuator operating mode. When passive front leveling is desired, the method includes opening a fluid communication path between the left front actuator and the right front actuator to permit fluid exchange therebetween. When active front leveling is desired, the method includes closing or restricting the fluid communication path and independently controlling the left front actuator and the right front actuator. The method may further include transitioning between the passive and active modes while maintaining pressure balance, limiting actuator stroke, detecting wheel unload, or preventing excessive chassis twist.

In certain implementations, the controller is configured to perform a leveling sequence in which the rear actuators are first adjusted to reduce roll of a rear portion of the chassis, after which the front actuators are either maintained in the coupled mode to passively conform to the ground or decoupled and actively adjusted to further reduce chassis pitch or roll. Alternatively, the controller may actively control all four actuators in a coordinated manner when high-precision leveling is required. The controller may also monitor actuator position and hydraulic pressure to identify a load distribution condition, and may inhibit lift elevation if the chassis tilt, actuator stroke, or support loading is outside predetermined limits.

The disclosed arrangement provides a hybrid leveling architecture in which two rear actuators provide active rear leveling and two front actuators provide selectable passive or active front leveling. By allowing the front actuators to be fluidly coupled during selected operating conditions, the system can reduce control complexity, improve terrain compliance, and maintain wheel contact. By decoupling the front actuators during other operating conditions, the system can provide enhanced stability and precise chassis attitude control suitable for lifting operations.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: In formal patent language, describe an embodiment of a lift device comprising a chassis, a rear leveling assembly, and a front leveling assembly, specifying how the actuators control pitch and roll adjustments.
counterfactuals.output:
In one embodiment, a lift device comprises a chassis defining a longitudinal axis and a lateral axis, the chassis being supported by a plurality of ground-engaging members. The lift device further comprises a rear leveling assembly operatively coupled to a rear portion of the chassis and a front leveling assembly operatively coupled to a front portion of the chassis.

The rear leveling assembly includes a first rear actuator and a second rear actuator laterally spaced from the first rear actuator. Each of the first rear actuator and the second rear actuator is configured to selectively extend and retract to adjust a relative height of a corresponding rear side of the chassis with respect to a support surface. The front leveling assembly includes a first front actuator and a second front actuator laterally spaced from the first front actuator. Each of the first front actuator and the second front actuator is configured to selectively extend and retract to adjust a relative height of a corresponding front side of the chassis with respect to the support surface.

In operation, coordinated actuation of the rear leveling assembly and the front leveling assembly is configured to adjust a pitch orientation of the chassis about the lateral axis. For example, extension of the front actuators relative to the rear actuators, or retraction of the rear actuators relative to the front actuators, raises the front portion of the chassis relative to the rear portion, thereby adjusting pitch in a first direction. Conversely, extension of the rear actuators relative to the front actuators, or retraction of the front actuators relative to the rear actuators, raises the rear portion of the chassis relative to the front portion, thereby adjusting pitch in an opposite direction.

The actuators are further configured to adjust a roll orientation of the chassis about the longitudinal axis. In particular, differential actuation between laterally opposed actuators adjusts the relative elevation of opposing sides of the chassis. For example, extension of actuators disposed on a first lateral side of the chassis relative to actuators disposed on a second lateral side of the chassis raises the first lateral side relative to the second lateral side, thereby adjusting roll in a first direction. Conversely, extension of the actuators disposed on the second lateral side relative to the actuators disposed on the first lateral side raises the second lateral side relative to the first lateral side, thereby adjusting roll in an opposite direction.

A controller may be operatively coupled to the first rear actuator, the second rear actuator, the first front actuator, and the second front actuator. The controller is configured to command selective extension and retraction of the actuators individually or in coordinated groups to level the chassis, to maintain the chassis at a desired pitch and roll orientation, or to compensate for uneven terrain during operation of the lift device.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4
